title: MambaSL: Single-Layer Mamba for Time Series Classification
one_liner: A one-layer state space model that picks which parts of a time series matter most, solving the underexplored question of whether Mamba can classify sequences on its own.
lead: Time series classification means watching a stream of numbers over time and predicting what they represent (like recognizing a heartbeat pattern from an ECG). Most recent advances used complicated models, but MambaSL asks: can a single-layer Mamba (a fast model for sequences) do the job just by learning which parts of the time series to focus on?

problem.h2: Time Series Classification: Watching a Stream and Making Sense
paras: A time series is just a sequence of numbers recorded one after another over time. To classify it, a model must look at the whole stream and decide what it represents. Older approaches tried complex stacked layers, recurrent networks that fed hidden state forward one step at a time, or models that compared every pair of time steps to each other.

The naive attempt: give the model all the numbers and train it to guess the class. But most time points are noise or irrelevant context. Without a way to focus on the truly informative moments, the model wastes capacity learning red herrings, and training becomes slow and results become weaker. State space models like Mamba were invented to handle long sequences efficiently, but almost no one had tested whether a bare single-layer Mamba could do time series classification alone.
The researchers noticed a gap: every published study of Mamba was either on language (tokens of text) or synthetic tasks, not on real time series data.

callout.html: MambaSL learns which parts of a time series matter most, then pools them into a decision.

paras: Most time series models process every step uniformly. MambaSL adds a learned gate: a small neural circuit that scores each time step and either passes its value or zeros it out. This gate is not hand-coded; the model learns which kinds of patterns in the data deserve high scores.

hidden.h2: Selectivity: Which Time Steps the Model Trusts
hidden.name: Per-step selection score
paras: The hidden quantity is how much weight the model assigns to each time step when deciding the class. If a step scores low, the model passes almost nothing from it to the decision. If high, the model pools that step's information into its final decision. This is not computed all at once; the state space model computes it step by step as it reads the sequence.

MambaSL learns these selection scores by gradient descent: on each training batch, steps that help predict the correct class get higher scores, while misleading or irrelevant steps get lower scores. The paper measures this by showing that the learned scores correlate with domain knowledge (e.g., in a medical time series, the gate selects the clinically informative beats, not the baseline noise).

heat.caption: Darker means the model assigns higher weight to that time step. Boxed steps are the critical moments.

reads.html: The model learns to ignore noise and focus on the parts of the time series that truly distinguish one class from another.
The selective SSM layer computes a per-step gate that modulates the hidden state update, implementing learned feature selectivity when the trained model makes predictions on new data.

paras: A raw time series has many ups and downs, most of which are noise. If the model treats every step equally, it must learn to recognize the class despite the noise, which requires a larger model and more training data to separate signal from junk. Selectivity flips this: instead of the model memorizing which noise patterns to ignore, it learns which signal patterns to attend to. This is simpler because good features are sparse: in most real time series, only a few percent of the steps contain the discriminative information.

The mechanism works in two stages. First, the state space model reads the time series in order, building up a summary at each step. Second, the learned gate applies a mask: scores near 1 let information through, scores near 0 block it. On the backward pass during training, gradients flow strongly into steps that the gate kept open and weak into steps the gate closed. The model learns to open the gate wide on steps that help predict the true class and close it on steps that don't, or worse, point toward a wrong class, because the loss (a measure of how wrong the prediction is) only shrinks when the gate lets through information that pushes the prediction toward the true answer.

This design is efficient: a single-layer state space model has far fewer learned numbers to adjust than a deep model with many stacked layers, so it trains faster and generalizes to smaller datasets. Selectivity lets that one layer focus its learning on the informative subset, avoiding the classic problem of deep networks: spreading the model's learned knowledge across irrelevant features.

stages.s: State space layer reads and summarizes (one at a time)

Gate output multiplies the state (high scores pass through, low scores zero out)
Pool selected time steps into a summary vector

bars.h2: Real-world performance: MambaSL vs. deep baselines

charts.title: Naive deep model (stacked layers, attends uniformly to all steps)
charts.note: Complex architecture but spreads capacity over all time steps equally, missing the opportunity to focus on signal.

charts.title: MambaSL (one layer with selective gate)
charts.note: Simpler design, but the selective gate lets the single layer learn an efficient representation by filtering noise.

items.html: If the time series changes character partway through (the class-relevant patterns shift), the gate trained on early data will keep selecting the old patterns and miss the new ones.

items.b: Tiny informative signal in a huge stream.
items.html: If only one anomalous spike in a 10,000-step sequence matters, selectivity still needs the model to find it. The gate helps, but the model must still see the whole series, because if a critical spike is hidden in the noise, the model's gradients during training may never guide it to focus on that exact spot unless it reads every part of the input.

On datasets where every time point contributes equally to the class (rare but possible), a selective gate learns gate scores near 0.5 for all steps, wasting capacity on a learned filter that does nothing. A full model without the gate would fare better, because if selectivity offers no advantage, the gate becomes a useless layer that the model must learn and carry, reducing the effective size of the one-layer architecture.

items.b: Done right: datasets with clear, sparse signal.
items.html: On real time series like sensor recordings, medical signals, or financial ticks, where a few key events dominate, the selective gate learns to isolate them, and MambaSL outperforms bigger models, because the single layer can now devote all its learning power to the true signal and skip the wasted learning on noise, whereas a large model spreads its capacity over both signal and noise and requires much more data to separate them.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small time series classification dataset (e.g. 20 examples per class, 100 time steps each). Train MambaSL for 50 epochs and also train a baseline deep model (three stacked layers without selectivity). On test data, log the class accuracy and the learned gate scores for each time step. Then, on a single test example, plot the time series and highlight (in color) the time steps that the gate gave high scores. The visualization should show that the gate concentrates on a small region or set of peaks, and that region matches human intuition for what makes the time series belong to that class. For instance, if the time series is a heartbeat pattern, the gate should highlight the QRS complex, not the baseline. If the accuracy gap favors MambaSL, you have shown that learning to focus works.
demo.metric_eq: Improvement = Accuracy(MambaSL) - Accuracy(deep baseline); Gate alignment = fraction of high-scored time steps that coincide with domain-labeled signal regions
demo.closing: The demo proves that a single learned gate can beat a much larger model because it lets the model focus learning on the sparse true signal, not spread capacity over noise.
